newsitem.title: UK: Strong UK credit figures argue against rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Strong UK credit figures argue against rate cut.

text.p: Buoyant UK consumer credit figures in July suggest there is little need to ease monetary policy further, analysts said on Friday.
But few were willing to discount completely an interest rate cut after next Wednesday's monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
"The consumer credit data...confirm the picture of a consumer-led recovery in the economy," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.

"As such, they argue against a further cut in interest rates," he added. Net consumer credit totalled 1.027 billion in July, well above June's 659 million stg and significantly above most economists' forecasts.

Warwick Lightfoot, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, said the weakness in British manufacturing, below par retail sales figures in July and slowing M4 money supply growth gave Clarke enough scope to keep rate cuts on the agenda.
"However...the retail sales data in July cannot be reconciled with either survey and anecdotal evidence of consumer spending or with the latest consumer credit data," he said.

Final M4 figures, released alongside the credit data at 0830 GMT, showed broad money growth of 9.0 percent year-on-year on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 10.1 percent in June and just back inside the government's monitoring range.

"The credit figures flies in the face of the last sales data and is more consistent with the anecdotal evidence that the sales environment is firm," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
UK retail sales fell 0.2 percent in July, taking the year-on-year rate of growth down to 2.2 percent, from 3.4 in June.
"I expect the anomoly is with the retail sales figures," Shepperd said, adding that the market had been expecting strong consumer credit figures -- but not that strong.
"The BBA figures indicated credit held up well in July but the extent of the rise was a surprise," he said. "It's only the second time it's been over a billion (stg)."
British Bankers' Association data, which offer an incomplete picture of credit demand, showed consumer borrowing of 539 million stg in July, more than double June's figure.
But Friday's figures may not tilt the monetary policy balance decisively either way.
"I don't think it's the sort of figure that is decisive for monetary policy but to the extent it has an influence it's certainly pro-Bank rather than pro Clarke," Shepperd said.
The Bank of England has argued against interest rate cuts for months now and disagreed with Clarke's decision to cut base rates by a quarter-point to 5.75 percent in June.
"Overall, the market will be looking for no change in interest rates next week but there will be plenty of people peering anxiously at their screens after the meeting ends," Shepperd said.

Short sterling futures were unchanged after the consumer credit figures were released but with the September and December contracts trading at 94.26 and 94.27 respectively, the strip is resolutely pricing in no change in interest rates out to the year-end.
